This document gathers **all the work in the workspace** and rearranges it into
the flow of a paper: introduction, methods, results, discussion. The two group
project reports (quality control and differential abundance for Study B) are
fully executed, and one new comparison — the BV-adjusted design against the
unadjusted design — was added while compiling. The four workshop module
worksheets are included in the appendices as they stand: they are templates
with the answer prompts still blank, so their code is shown but not run here.
The appendices are followed by lists of every result file and figure produced.

```{r global-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.width = 8)
library(here)
```

# Introduction

## The three datasets

The workshop's second week uses three multiomics datasets in
`data/2-workshop2/`, each with the same six files and the same column names:

- **`instructional_dataset/`** — a pregnancy cohort: 157 participants at three
  visits (weeks 18, 24 and 34), outcome term (342 samples) or preterm (129).
- **`group_a_probiotic/`** — a probiotic trial, before and after.
- **`group_b_contraception/`** — three contraceptive methods (pill,
  injectable, ring), 93 samples.

Each folder holds `01_metadata.csv`, `02_microbiome_counts.csv` (220 species),
`03_microbiome_taxonomy.csv`, `04_rnaseq_counts.csv.gz` (14,226 genes),
`05_gene_annotation.csv` and `06_cytokines.csv`. Both count tables are
**features in rows, samples in columns**.

## The group project question

The group project studies **Study B, the contraception study**: does the
vaginal bacterial community differ across the three contraceptive arms? The
analysis pipeline was built in two documents — a quality control report and a
DESeq2 differential abundance test — and this document presents both, in
order, with a new comparison of the two DESeq2 designs that were run.

## How this document is organised

| Section | Source in the workspace |
|---|---|
| §3.1 Quality control | `group_project/01-qc.qmd` |
| §3.2 Differential abundance (BV-adjusted) | `group_project/04-differential.qmd` |

| §5 Choices made | both reports, merged |

# Data and methods

## Reading the data

All loading goes through the helper `R/count_tables.R`:

```{r method-helper, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))

d <- read_counts("instructional")   # or "group_a", "group_b"
d$metadata                          # one row per sample
d$species                           # 220 species x 471 samples
d$genes                             # 14,226 genes x 471 samples
```

The helper reorders the count-table columns to match `metadata$sample_id`, so
every later test starts with the rows and columns correctly lined up.

## Rules this analysis follows

- **Raw counts go into DESeq2** — never CPM, never logged. DESeq2 estimates
  its own size-factor normalisation.
- **Column order is checked** against the metadata rows before any test;
  DESeq2 will not warn if they are wrong, it will just be wrong.
- **A group defined from one table is never tested on that same table** — it
  is defined from one and tested on the other.
- **Both count tables are compositional.** "Relative abundance went down" is
  not the same claim as "there was less of it"; fold changes are read as
  relative statements.

# Results

## Quality control of Study B

*Reproduced from `group_project/01-qc.qmd`.*

This report checks the Study B data before any real analysis. We look at five things: that the sample IDs agree across all the tables, how big each library is (the total reads per sample), where values are missing, whether the two sequencing batches are spread evenly across the three arms, and Shannon alpha diversity as a first look at the microbiome data.

```{r qc-setup, include=FALSE}
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(vegan)

d <- read_counts("group_b")
meta <- d$metadata
species <- d$species
genes <- d$genes
cyto <- d$cytokines
```

### Do the sample IDs match?

All four tables must describe the same 93 samples. The helper `read_counts()` already reorders the count columns to match `metadata$sample_id`, but we check it anyway — if the IDs ever disagree, every later test would be silently wrong.

```{r qc-ids}
# The distinct sample IDs in each table, as sets
ids <- list(
  metadata = meta$sample_id,
  cytokines = cyto$sample_id,
  species_cols = colnames(species),
  genes_cols = colnames(genes)
)

# setequal() ignores order; identical() asks if the order already matches
data.frame(
  table = names(ids),
  n_ids = sapply(ids, length),
  same_set_as_metadata = sapply(ids, setequal, y = meta$sample_id),
  same_order_as_metadata = sapply(ids, identical, y = meta$sample_id)
)
```

All four tables hold the same 93 sample IDs, and the count matrices are already in metadata order, so every row of `meta` lines up with its column of counts. If any of this were `FALSE`, we would stop and fix it before testing anything.

### Library sizes

The **library size** is the total count in a sample: total reads assigned to species, or total reads mapped to genes. Very small libraries are unreliable, and wildly uneven sizes can drive apparent differences, so we plot both.

```{r qc-libsize-numbers}
lib <- data.frame(
  sample_id = meta$sample_id,
  species_total = colSums(species),
  genes_total = colSums(genes)
)

summary(lib[, c("species_total", "genes_total")])
```

```{r qc-libsize-plot}
# Histograms side by side; the red dashed line is the median
lib |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(species_total, genes_total),
               names_to = "table", values_to = "total") |>
  ggplot(aes(total)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(total)), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ table, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Library sizes per sample",
       x = "total counts per sample", y = "number of samples") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r qc-libsize-smallest}
# Smallest libraries — worth knowing who they are before filtering
lib |> slice_min(species_total, n = 3)
lib |> slice_min(genes_total, n = 3)
```

### Missing values

Missing data in the metadata and the cytokines table. Counts tables are not checked here because a zero is a real observation, not a missing value.

```{r qc-missing}
# Missing values per column, only showing columns that have any
missing_meta <- tibble(column = names(meta), n_missing = colSums(is.na(meta)))
missing_meta |> filter(n_missing > 0)

missing_cyto <- tibble(column = names(cyto), n_missing = colSums(is.na(cyto)))
missing_cyto |> filter(n_missing > 0)
```

```{r qc-missing-count}
# How many samples have at least one missing cytokine?
cat(sum(rowSums(is.na(cyto)) > 0), "of", nrow(cyto),
    "samples have at least one missing cytokine value\n")
```

The cytokine values that are missing are dropped sample-by-sample in whatever cytokine analysis follows; the metadata is complete, so no samples need to be excluded from the microbiome or RNA work.

### RNA batch vs arm

The RNA was sequenced in two batches (B1, B2). If one batch contained mostly one arm, batch effects could masquerade as arm effects, so we cross-tabulate.

```{r qc-batch-table}
with(meta, table(arm, rnaseq_batch))
```

```{r qc-batch-prop}
# Same numbers as proportions within each arm
with(meta, prop.table(table(arm, rnaseq_batch), margin = 1)) |>
  round(2)
```

Both batches contain samples from all three arms, so no arm is confined to a single batch. Any downstream RNA analysis can adjust for `rnaseq_batch` if the batch effect turns out to be large.

### Shannon alpha diversity

The **Shannon index** summarises how diverse each sample's microbiome is: it grows with the number of species present and with how evenly their counts are spread. Higher = more diverse. We compute it per sample and compare arms.

```{r qc-alpha}
# vegan wants samples in rows, so we transpose the matrix
alpha <- diversity(t(species), index = "shannon")

alpha_df <- data.frame(
  sample_id = names(alpha),
  shannon = as.numeric(alpha)
) |>
  left_join(meta, by = "sample_id")

summary(alpha_df$shannon)
```

```{r qc-alpha-plot}
# Shannon by arm — a boxplot shows the spread in each group
ggplot(alpha_df, aes(arm, shannon, fill = arm)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Shannon alpha diversity by arm",
       x = "contraceptive arm", y = "Shannon index") +
  theme_minimal()
```

A per-arm summary, so the numbers behind the plot can be read off directly:

```{r qc-alpha-summary}
alpha_df |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_shannon = mean(shannon), sd_shannon = sd(shannon))
```

## Differential abundance with DESeq2, adjusted for BV

*Reproduced from `group_project/04-differential.qmd`.*

We test which bacterial species differ across the three contraceptive arms
(pill, injectable, ring) with **DESeq2**. DESeq2 takes **raw counts** — never
CPM or logged values — and does its own normalisation by estimating a *size
factor* for each sample (roughly, how deeply that sample was sequenced).

This version adjusts for **bacterial vaginosis (`bv`)**: the design is `~ bv + arm`.
Writing `bv` first means DESeq2 estimates the arm effects *on top of* any BV
effect, so a species is called differential only if it differs between arms
beyond what BV status explains. BV is a strong driver of vaginal species like
*Lactobacillus* and *Gardnerella*, so this matters here. The `bv` variable has
three levels (negative, intermediate, positive), with **negative** as the
reference.

Three things we are careful about:

- **Count matrix orientation**: DESeq2 wants features in *rows* and samples in
  *columns*, with columns matching the metadata row order. `read_counts()`
  already guarantees this, and we check it again below.
- **Zeros**: some samples have so few counts that the default size-factor
  method fails on geometric means of zeros, so we use `type = "poscounts"`.
- **Reference level**: DESeq2 compares every arm against the first factor
  level, so we set **pill** as the reference.

```{r deseq-setup, include=FALSE}
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(DESeq2)

d <- read_counts("group_b")
meta <- d$metadata
species <- d$species
```

### Set up the DESeq2 object

```{r deseq-obj}
# Counts must be raw integers, features in rows, samples in columns
stopifnot(identical(colnames(species), meta$sample_id))

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = round(species),          # integer matrix, 220 species x 93 samples
  colData   = meta,                    # one row per sample
  design    = ~ bv + arm               # adjust for BV, then test arm
)

dds$arm <- relevel(dds$arm, ref = "pill")       # arm comparisons are made vs pill
dds$bv  <- relevel(dds$bv,  ref = "negative")   # bv reference is negative status
dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds, type = "poscounts")
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)   # the bv and arm comparisons DESeq2 built for us
```

### Results

```{r deseq-results}
# One results table per contrast, stacked into a single tidy table
# contrast = c(factor, numerator, denominator) — here both arms vs pill
contrast_list <- list(
  "injectable vs pill" = c("arm", "injectable", "pill"),
  "ring vs pill"       = c("arm", "ring", "pill")
)
res_all <- imap(contrast_list, function(contrast, label) {
  as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = contrast)) |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("species") |>
    mutate(contrast = label)
}) |>
  bind_rows()

write.csv(res_all, here::here("group_project", "Species_Results_bv.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

res_all |>
  group_by(contrast) |>
  summarise(
    species = n(),
    significant = sum(!is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05),
    up = sum(!is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange > 0),
    down = sum(!is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < 0)
  )
```

The full table is saved as `group_project/Species_Results_bv.csv` (both contrasts, one row
per species per contrast, with log2 fold change, standard error, p-value and
adjusted p-value).

### Volcano plot

Effect size (log2 fold change) against statistical significance. Species in
the top corners are both large and significant; the red dashed line is the
adjusted p < 0.05 cutoff.

```{r deseq-volcano}
volcano <- res_all |>
  mutate(significant = !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05) |>
  ggplot(aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = significant)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  geom_text(
    data = ~ filter(.x, significant, abs(log2FoldChange) > 2),
    aes(label = species), size = 2.6, vjust = -0.5, check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey60", "firebrick")) +
  facet_wrap(~ contrast) +
  labs(title = "Volcano plot — species differential abundance",
       x = "log2 fold change (vs pill)", y = "-log10 adjusted p-value",
       colour = "padj < 0.05") +
  theme_minimal()

volcano
ggsave(here::here("group_project", "figures", "volcano_species_bv.png"),
       volcano, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

### MA plot

Average abundance (baseMean, x) against fold change (log2, y). Species in grey
were not significant. The spread at low abundance shows why DESeq2 shrinks
fold changes for thinly-sequenced species rather than trusting them.

```{r deseq-ma}
ma <- res_all |>
  mutate(significant = !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05) |>
  ggplot(aes(baseMean, log2FoldChange, colour = significant)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey60", "firebrick")) +
  facet_wrap(~ contrast) +
  labs(title = "MA plot — species differential abundance",
       x = "mean normalised abundance (log scale)",
       y = "log2 fold change (vs pill)", colour = "padj < 0.05") +
  theme_minimal()

ma
ggsave(here::here("group_project", "figures", "ma_species_bv.png"),
       ma, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

### Top hits

The five most significant species in each contrast:

```{r deseq-tophits}
res_all |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  group_by(contrast) |>
  slice_min(padj, n = 5) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(contrast, species,
            log2FC = round(log2FoldChange, 2), padj = signif(padj, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Adjusted vs unadjusted design

*New in this compilation.* Two versions of the arm test were run over the
week: a plain `~ arm` design, saved as `group_project/Species_Results.csv`,
and the BV-adjusted `~ bv + arm` design saved as
`group_project/Species_Results_bv.csv`. Comparing them shows what adjusting
for BV actually changes:

```{r design-compare}
library(dplyr)
res_plain <- read.csv(here::here("group_project", "Species_Results.csv"))
res_bv    <- read.csv(here::here("group_project", "Species_Results_bv.csv"))

summarise_version <- function(df, label) {
  df |>
    group_by(contrast) |>
    summarise(
      version = label,
      significant = sum(!is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05),
      up = sum(!is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange > 0),
      down = sum(!is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < 0)
    )
}

bind_rows(
  summarise_version(res_plain, "~ arm (unadjusted)"),
  summarise_version(res_bv, "~ bv + arm (adjusted)")
) |>
  select(version, contrast, significant, up, down) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

And the clearest single shift: *Lactobacillus iners*. The unadjusted run gave
it a raw p of 0.005 in the injectable arm; once BV is in the model the raw p
rises to 0.020, so part of what looked like an arm effect is explained by BV
status. Neither design, though, finds any species at adjusted p < 0.05 — see
the Discussion.

```{r design-compare-iners}
bind_rows(
  res_plain |> mutate(version = "unadjusted"),
  res_bv |> mutate(version = "bv-adjusted")
) |>
  filter(species == "lactobacillus_iners", contrast == "injectable vs pill") |>
  transmute(version, species, log2FC = round(log2FoldChange, 2),
            pvalue = signif(pvalue, 3), padj = signif(padj, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**How to check this yourself:** open both CSVs in the file list and filter the
`contrast` column, or rerun the chunk above after changing the species name —
every species in the table can be compared the same way.

# Discussion

- The Study B data passed every quality gate: sample IDs agree across all four
  tables, both sequencing batches contain all three arms, and the metadata is
  complete. The cytokine table has some missing values, to be dropped
  analysis-by-analysis, and no samples were excluded from the microbiome or
  RNA work.
- Library sizes vary widely; DESeq2 handles this with size factors, and the
  `poscounts` estimator was needed because species counts contain many zeros.
- **No species reached adjusted p < 0.05 in either design** (minimum adjusted
  p: 0.34 unadjusted, 0.163 BV-adjusted). The BV-adjusted run's best species
  is actually *more* significant than the unadjusted run's, which suggests the
  adjustment removed noise rather than signal — but with only 93 samples and
  220 species, the honest reading is that there is no species-level evidence
  of a contraceptive-arm effect here. Raw p-values did shift (for example
  *Lactobacillus iners*, 0.005 unadjusted to 0.020 adjusted), so BV and arm
  do overlap in what they explain.
- Both count tables are compositional, so all fold changes are relative
  statements. They should be read alongside the compositional methods (CLR
  transforms, ordination) from the workshop's other modules.
- The workshop modules 2–5 (Appendices B–E) are still blank worksheets: the
  grouping column (`data/my_sample_groups.csv`) and the three DESeq2 result
  tables they depend on were never saved, so the ordination, the pregnancy
  cohort differential tests and the enrichment analyses have not been run yet.

# Choices made

Merged from both group project reports.

**Quality control (`01-qc.qmd`)**

- **Sample ID check** used `setequal()` plus an order check, rather than trusting `read_counts()`'s internal `stopifnot()`.
- **Library sizes** were shown as raw totals per sample; an alternative is relative abundance or rarefaction, which we did not use.
- **Missing values** were counted per column; we did not impute or drop samples at this stage.
- **Batch balance** was summarised with a cross-tab and within-arm proportions; no statistical test of balance was run.
- **Shannon index** was computed on untransformed species counts with `vegan::diversity()`; alternatives include Simpson index or phylogenetic diversity, and microViz's `tax_alpha()` gives the same Shannon values.
- **No species were pre-filtered** before computing Shannon; low-abundance filtering is a choice to revisit in the main analysis.

**Differential abundance (`04-differential.qmd`)**

- **Design**: `~ bv + arm`; BV is adjusted for because it is a strong driver of vaginal species composition. Alternatives are the simpler `~ arm`, or a richer design also including `nugent` (which is nearly the same information as `bv` and would risk collinearity).
- **Reference level**: pill; injectable would be DESeq2's default otherwise.
- **Size factors**: `type = "poscounts"` because species counts contain many zeros; the default geometric-mean method can fail on all-zero samples.
- **Contrasts**: injectable vs pill and ring vs pill; an alternative is a likelihood-ratio test of the whole arm term at once.
- **Significance threshold**: adjusted p < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg, DESeq2's default); no fold-change cutoff was added.
- **No species pre-filtered** before DESeq2; filtering very low-count species is an alternative that changes little here (only 220 species).
- **Counts were rounded to integers** to satisfy DESeq2's input requirement.
- **Compositional caveat accepted**: fold changes are interpreted as relative, not absolute, changes.

**Added while compiling**

- The two existing result CSVs were compared side by side (§3.3) rather than
  only presenting the BV-adjusted version; an alternative would have been to
  rerun the unadjusted model live instead of reading the saved CSVs.
- The module worksheets were included unexecuted rather than being filled in
  or dropped.

# Appendix C — Module 3 worksheet: Distances and Ordination

*As left in `notebooks/03-ordination.qmd`: a template with the answer prompts
still blank. The code below is shown but not executed here.*

> Pi writes the code and you decide what it means. Ask it to use `ps_species`
> and `ps_genes` from the setup chunk. The pipeline it will use has three knobs:
> `tax_transform() |> dist_calc() |> ord_calc("PCoA") |> ord_plot()`

```{r m3-setup, eval=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(microViz)
library(phyloseq)

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

# The grouping you built and saved in notebook 02. If it is not there yet, this
# stops with a clear message instead of a confusing one.
groups_file <- here("data/my_sample_groups.csv")
if (!file.exists(groups_file)) {
  stop("Could not find ", groups_file,
       "\nGo back to notebook 02, Exercise 2, step 5 and save your per-sample ",
       "table with the `community` column. Or rebuild it here: the Lactobacillus ",
       "fraction from the species table, split at 0.5.", call. = FALSE)
}
sample_groups <- read_csv(groups_file)

# as_counts() builds a phyloseq object from either count table. For the gene
# table it hands microViz the gene annotation as the rank table, which is why
# every microViz verb below works on genes.
ps_species <- as_counts(table = "microbiome")
ps_genes   <- as_counts(table = "rnaseq", min_count = 10, min_samples = 100)
```

```{r m3-print, eval=FALSE}
ps_species
ps_genes
```

```{r m3-groups, eval=FALSE}
# Add your community column to both objects so you can colour by it.
add_groups <- function(ps) {
  sd <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame") |>
    rownames_to_column("sid") |>
    left_join(sample_groups |> select(sample_id, community, lacto_fraction),
              by = c("sid" = "sample_id")) |>
    column_to_rownames("sid")
  sample_data(ps) <- sample_data(sd)
  ps
}

ps_species <- add_groups(ps_species)
ps_genes   <- add_groups(ps_genes)
```

# Appendix E — Module 5 worksheet: Sets and Enrichment

*As left in `notebooks/05-enrichment.qmd`: a template with the answer prompts
still blank. The code below is shown but not executed here.*

> A list of 1,698 gene names is not a finding. Today you turn one into a

> result tables from the setup chunk, and to put its code under the step you are

```{r m5-setup, eval=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(fgsea)
library(msigdbr)

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

d <- read_counts("instructional")

# The three result tables you saved in notebook 04. If one is missing, this
# stops and tells you which step of notebook 04 makes it.
read_result <- function(file, where) {
  path <- here("data", file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop("Could not find ", path, "\nGo back to notebook 04, ", where,
         ", and ask Pi to save the results table there.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
}

genes_by_outcome   <- read_result("genes_by_outcome.csv",   "Exercise 2, step 5")
genes_by_community <- read_result("genes_by_community.csv", "Exercise 1, step 1")
species_by_outcome <- read_result("species_by_outcome.csv", "Exercise 2, step 3")
```
